summary: Singapore is a city-state at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, independent since 1965 and known for its status as an international financial and shipping hub, its diverse ethnic groups and its efficient governance.

ranking.name: Buddhism
ranking.description: Buddhism was brought mainly by the large numbers of Chinese who migrated from Fujian, Guangdong, Teochew and Hainan after Raffles established the port of Singapore in 1819. The beliefs of the early Chinese were mostly a mixture of Buddhism, Daoism and folk religion; from the 1980s, with the spread of education and a movement toward religious orthodoxy, many Chinese moved from folk religion to explicitly identifying as Buddhists, making Buddhism the largest religion. From the 1960s a number of Theravada and Tibetan Buddhist groups also came to Singapore, but the followers are still mainly Chinese.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Singapore's non-religious population rose from 13% in 1980 to 20% in 2020, mainly English-educated young Chinese. Singapore's English-medium education emphasizes the practical and the scientific, and together with the government's secular policies this has led some young people to no longer identify with their parents' generation's folk religion. The proportion of non-religious people is especially high among the highly educated and high earners.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Christianity was introduced during British colonial rule in the 19th century; St Andrew's Church was completed in the 1830s, and Catholic, Anglican, Methodist and Presbyterian missionaries made schools their main instrument, such as the Anglo-Chinese School founded in 1886. In the 1980s and 1990s, large numbers of the English-educated Chinese middle class converted to Christianity, especially to large evangelical and charismatic churches, raising the Christian share from about one tenth in 1980 to nearly one fifth today.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam is the religion of Singapore's Malays, who are Singapore's indigenous people and lived here before Raffles arrived. Muslim merchants who migrated from southern India and Arab Hadhramaut in the 19th century also brought Islam, and the Sultan Mosque, built in 1824, is one of the oldest mosques. The Islamic Religious Council, established in 1968, is responsible for managing Muslim affairs, and Muslims are mainly Malays and some Indians.

ranking.name: Taoism and folk religion
ranking.description: Daoism and folk religion were brought by Chinese immigrants in the 19th century, and each dialect group built its own temples and clan associations, such as the Thian Hock Keng Temple built by the Hokkien in the 1840s, which is dedicated to Mazu. As younger generations received English-language education, the transmission of folk religion gradually weakened and many converted to Buddhism or Christianity, so that the share of Daoism and folk religion fell from about thirty percent in 1980 to less than ten percent today.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: Hinduism was brought mainly by Tamil laborers and merchants who migrated from southern India during British colonial rule in the 19th century, working in the port, on the railways and on plantations. The Sri Mariamman Temple, built in 1827, is Singapore's oldest Hindu temple. Thaipusam and Deepavali each year are important Hindu festivals, and Deepavali is also a public holiday in Singapore.

religion.background: Before Raffles founded the port in 1819, Singapore was a Malay fishing village whose inhabitants were Muslim. During British colonial rule large numbers of Chinese and Indians migrated in, bringing Buddhism, Daoism, folk religion and Hinduism, while missionaries brought Christianity. After independence in 1965 the government stressed religious harmony, and in 1990 passed the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act, prohibiting religious groups from getting involved in politics or inciting religious antagonism. Today Singapore is one of the most religiously diverse countries in the world.

language.official: English, Mandarin Chinese, Malay and Tamil are the official languages, and Malay is the national language.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English was the language of administration during British colonial rule (1819–1963). After independence in 1965 the government adopted English as the neutral common language among the ethnic groups, and in 1987 all schools nationwide made English the first language of instruction. This policy caused the use of English in homes to increase rapidly, and by 2020 nearly half of the population mainly spoke English at home, surpassing Mandarin. Singapore English (Singlish) blends vocabulary from Hokkien, Malay and other languages and is a distinctive language of everyday life.

ranking.name: Mandarin Chinese
ranking.description: The spread of Mandarin in Singapore came mainly from the 'Speak Mandarin Campaign' promoted by Lee Kuan Yew in 1979, in which the government encouraged Chinese to give up their various dialects and speak Mandarin, in order to unify the Chinese community's language and maintain economic ties with China. Mandarin is the mother-tongue subject in schools, but as English has spread, the proportion of young Chinese who speak English at home has continued to rise.

ranking.name: Other Chinese dialects (Hokkien, etc.)
ranking.description: Dialects such as Hokkien, Cantonese, Teochew, Hakka and Hainanese are the home-region languages of Chinese immigrants since the 19th century and were once the main languages of Singapore's Chinese community. After the Speak Mandarin Campaign of 1979, television and radio were forbidden from broadcasting dialect programs and schools did not teach dialects, so dialect use dropped sharply and is mainly among the elderly. In recent years the government has relaxed dialect programming to a limited extent to cater to the elderly.

ranking.name: Malay
ranking.description: Malay is Singapore's national language because the Malays are Singapore's indigenous people and because Singapore briefly joined Malaysia in 1963–1965. The national anthem 'Majulah Singapura' is sung in Malay, and military commands are also given in Malay. Malay is mainly used in Malay households and accounts for about one tenth of the population.

ranking.name: Tamil
ranking.description: Tamil was brought by the Tamil laborers and merchants who migrated from southern India in the 19th century; Indians make up about 9% of Singapore's population, most of them Tamil, so Tamil was made one of the four official languages. But as English has spread, more and more Indian families speak English at home.

language.history: Before the port was founded in 1819, Malay was dominant in Singapore. During British colonial rule the Chinese, Indians and Malays each used their own languages, with Malay the common language of the marketplace and English the language of administration. After independence in 1965 the government pursued a bilingual policy, with English as the common language and each group's mother tongue as the second language. The Speak Mandarin Campaign of 1979 made Mandarin replace the dialects, and in 1987 schools were unified under English-medium teaching, so English gradually became the main home language.

ranking.name: Hainanese chicken rice
ranking.description: Rice is cooked in chicken broth with chicken fat, ginger, garlic and pandan leaves into a richly fragrant rice, served with poached or roast chicken, and eaten with chili sauce, ginger paste and dark soy sauce.
ranking.history: Hainanese chicken rice originated from the 'Wenchang chicken' of Wenchang on Hainan Island and was brought to Singapore by Hainanese immigrants in the first half of the 20th century. Early Hainanese mostly worked in catering and as cooks; they adapted their hometown method, cooking the rice in chicken broth and adding Southeast Asian pandan leaves and chili sauce. In the 1940s and 1950s Wang Yiyuan ran a chicken rice stall in Singapore, making Hainanese chicken rice widely popular. It is generally regarded as Singapore's national dish, and Singapore and Malaysia often dispute its origin.

ranking.name: Chili crab
ranking.description: Whole crabs are stir-fried in a sweet and spicy sauce made from ketchup, chili sauce, egg ribbons and sugar, with a thick sauce, and fried mantou buns are used to dip in the sauce.
ranking.history: Chili crab is generally thought to have been invented in the 1950s by Mdm Cher Yam Tian of Singapore and her husband at a roadside stall; she tried adding ketchup and chili sauce to steamed crab, which was very popular, and she later opened a restaurant. In the 1960s another chef added egg ribbons, giving rise to today's version. It is Singapore's most representative seafood dish and is often listed in tourism promotion as a must-eat food.

ranking.name: Laksa
ranking.description: A rich curry soup base made from coconut milk, chili, lemongrass, dried shrimp and laksa leaves is served with rice vermicelli, shrimp, fish cake, blood cockles and bean sprouts, with a fragrant, spicy and rich flavor.
ranking.history: Laksa is representative of 'Nyonya' (Peranakan) cuisine; the Peranakans are descendants of Chinese immigrants who have intermarried with Malays since the 15th century and who blended Chinese and Malay cooking methods. The Katong district in eastern Singapore is a Peranakan neighborhood, and 'Katong laksa' is known for its cut short noodles that can be eaten with just a spoon, making it Singapore's most famous version of laksa.

ranking.name: Bak kut teh
ranking.description: A soup of pork ribs simmered with pepper, garlic and spices; the Singapore version has a clear broth with a strong pepper flavor, often served with fried dough sticks and white rice, and gongfu tea is drunk after the meal to cut the greasiness.
ranking.history: Bak kut teh originated with Chinese dockworkers who migrated to Singapore from Fujian and Teochew in the 19th and early 20th centuries, who drank this soup in the early morning before work to restore their strength. Singapore is dominated by the Teochew-style clear pepper version, while the Klang area of Malaysia is known for the Hokkien-style dark herbal broth. The 'tea' in the name refers to the Chinese tea served with it, used to cut the greasiness of the pork.

ranking.name: Char kway teow
ranking.description: Flat rice noodles are stir-fried over high heat with shrimp, Chinese sausage, fish cake, blood cockles, bean sprouts and egg, with dark soy sauce and lard, giving a smoky 'wok hei' and a charred aroma.
ranking.history: Char kway teow came from Teochew and Hokkien immigrants, and 'kway teow' is the Hokkien name for flat rice noodles. In the early 20th century it was a cheap meal for dockworkers and laborers, stir-fried in lard to provide plenty of calories at low cost. Today it is one of the most popular dishes at Singapore's hawker centres, and in 2020 Singapore's hawker culture was inscribed by UNESCO on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
